title: How we calculate in this app
body:
Numerology has no single, universal way of calculating. Different schools and authors use different rules, so we want to describe clearly the convention adopted in this app.

The basic operation is reduction: adding the digits of a number until a single digit is left. For example, 35 gives 3 + 5 = 8. The exceptions are the so-called master numbers: 11, 22 and 33. Wherever they are allowed, we stop the reduction and leave the value as it is.

We calculate the life path by adding all the digits of the full date of birth at once. For 14.07.1985 we add 1 + 4 + 0 + 7 + 1 + 9 + 8 + 5, which gives 35, and 8 after reduction. Sums of 11, 22 and 33 stay unchanged.

The birthday number is the day of the month after reduction. Day 14 gives 5, and day 29 gives 11, which we keep. Here we keep only 11 and 22.

The numbers from the full name are based on a cyclical letter table: A = 1, B = 2 and so on up to I = 9, then J = 1 up to R = 9, and then S = 1 up to Z = 8. Polish letters are replaced by their base letters: Ą by A, Ć by C, Ę by E, Ł by L, Ń by N, Ó by O, Ś by S, and Ź and Ż by Z. We count A, E, I, O, U and Y as vowels and treat all the other letters as consonants.

The expression number comes from the sum of all the letters, the soul urge number from the vowels alone, and the personality number from the consonants. For the name Łucja, changed to LUCJA, we get L = 3, U = 3, C = 3, J = 1, A = 1. All the letters give 11, the vowels U and A give 4, and the consonants L, C and J give 7. In these three numbers we also keep 11, 22 and 33.

We calculate the personal year by adding the digits of the day of birth, the month of birth and the chosen calendar year, and the result is always reduced to the range 1 to 9. For a person born on 14 July and the year 2026 we have 1 + 4 + 0 + 7 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 6 = 22, which for this number we reduce further to 4.

It is worth knowing that other schools do this differently. Some authors first reduce the day, month and year separately and only then add the results, which can change whether a master number appears. Some treat Y as a consonant, or decide by how it sounds, and others count the personal year from the birthday instead of from 1 January. Each of these decisions can give a different result. No convention is truer than the others, because they all belong to a symbolic tradition, not to science.

Sources: Underwood Dudley, “Numerology: Or What Pythagoras Wrought”, Mathematical Association of America, 1997; Juno Jordan, “Numerology: The Romance in Your Name”, 1965.

title: A short history of numerology
body:
The fascination with numbers is very old. In many ancient cultures numbers had not only a practical meaning but also a religious and symbolic one. The example most often cited is the Pythagoreans, a philosophical community associated with Pythagoras of Samos, active in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE in southern Italy.

We know surprisingly little about Pythagoras himself, because none of his writings survive and many accounts were written several centuries later. Historians stress that it is hard to separate his actual views from the legend that grew up around him. We do know, however, that in the Pythagorean circle numbers were regarded as the key to understanding the order of the world; they were linked with musical harmony and given qualities, with even and odd, for example, associated with opposites.

Number symbolism went on developing later too: in Neoplatonic philosophy, in medieval theology, in the Jewish tradition of gematria, in which Hebrew letters were given numerical values, and in Renaissance Hermetic thought. Each of these traditions had its own assumptions and aims, so they should not be treated as one continuous numerology.

Modern numerology, with its life path, expression number and letter table from 1 to 9, is a relatively young phenomenon. According to the available studies, its popular form took shape around the turn of the 20th century, mainly in English-speaking countries. The American author L. Dow Balliett, who published works on the meaning of numbers and letters around 1908, is often mentioned here, along with Juno Jordan, usually presented as continuing her work, whose 1965 book helped to spread the system. The details of this genealogy are told in different ways, so they are best treated with caution.

The name “Pythagorean numerology” is therefore more of a tribute to an ancient tradition than a description of its actual origin. There is no evidence that the Pythagoreans used a table of Latin letters in the way today's handbooks do.

Two things are worth keeping apart. The history of numerology is a real and interesting cultural subject. But the fact that a practice has a long history does not mean that its predictions or character descriptions have been scientifically confirmed. Researchers and science communicators, such as the mathematician Underwood Dudley, point out that numerology has no empirical basis. In the app we treat it as a language of symbols that can inspire reflection, not as a source of knowledge about the future.

Sources: Walter Burkert, “Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism”, Harvard University Press, 1972; Christoph Riedweg, “Pythagoras: His Life, Teaching, and Influence”, Cornell University Press, 2005; Underwood Dudley, “Numerology: Or What Pythagoras Wrought”, Mathematical Association of America, 1997.

title: A short history of tarot
body:
Today tarot is associated above all with fortune-telling, but its beginnings were quite different. Card historians agree that tarot decks came into being in northern Italy in the 15th century as playing cards. They were then called carte da trionfi, cards of the triumphs, and later tarocchi.

A series of cards with allegorical images, which acted as trumps in the game, was added to an ordinary deck of four suits. The best-known early decks are the hand-painted cards connected with the Visconti and Sforza families of Milan, dating from the middle of the 15th century. The game of tarot then spread across Europe, and in some countries, such as France and Austria, it is still played today.

The turning point came in the 18th century. In 1781 the French scholar Antoine Court de Gébelin published, in one of the volumes of his work “Le Monde primitif”, the claim that tarot was a record of ancient Egyptian wisdom. The claim had no historical basis, and the decipherment of hieroglyphs in the following century showed that there is no connection between the cards and Egyptian writing. Even so, the idea proved very influential. Soon afterwards Jean-Baptiste Alliette, known as Etteilla, began to publish decks and handbooks intended for fortune-telling.

In the 19th century tarot became an important part of European occultism. The French author Éliphas Lévi linked the Major Arcana with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet and with Kabbalah. At the end of the century the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1888, was active in Britain and developed its own system of card symbolism.

Arthur Edward Waite came from the circle of this order. The deck published in 1909 by the London publisher William Rider & Son was created under his direction. The illustrations were made by the artist Pamela Colman Smith. What was new was that not only the trumps but also the numbered cards of the Minor Arcana were given scenes with figures, which made the images easier to interpret. For a long time the deck was named after the publisher and Waite, while Smith's contribution stayed in the shadows. Today the name Rider–Waite–Smith is used more and more often, to give credit to the creator of the images that became the model for hundreds of later decks.

The history of tarot shows how the same object can change its meaning from one era to another: from a game, through an occult symbol, to a tool for present-day reflection. In the app we use this wealth of images as an inspiration for thought, not as a way of predicting the future.

Sources: Michael Dummett, “The Game of Tarot”, Duckworth, 1980; Ronald Decker, Thierry Depaulis, Michael Dummett, “A Wicked Pack of Cards: The Origins of the Occult Tarot”, 1996; Helen Farley, “A Cultural History of Tarot”, I.B. Tauris, 2009; Arthur Edward Waite, “The Pictorial Key to the Tarot”, 1910.

title: How to use the cards for reflection
body:
In this app we treat tarot cards as a mirror made of images. They do not tell you what will happen, and they know nothing about you that you do not bring to the conversation with them yourself. Their strength is that rich symbolism stirs associations and helps you look at a familiar situation from a slightly different side.

It is good to start with an open question. Instead of asking whether something will work out, you can ask what deserves your attention, or what you can learn in this situation. Questions like these do not ask the cards for a prediction, and they leave you room for your own conclusions.

After drawing a card, pause for a moment with the image itself before you read the description. What do you see first? What is the mood of the scene? Who is in it and what are they doing? Your spontaneous impression can be just as valuable as the card's traditional meaning. The description in the app is one possible interpretation, not the only truth.

In spreads of several cards, each position has a question assigned to it, for example: what is the background to the matter, what is the challenge, what small step could you consider. Treat these positions as just that: questions that give your thinking a structure, not verdicts. If a card in a given position does not seem to fit, that is information too. Perhaps the question is worth asking differently.

Reversed cards, those that come out upside down, are read in different ways in the tradition. Some people see in them the muted or blocked energy of the card, others an invitation to look at the theme from the inside, and others again do not use reversals at all. A reversed card does not mean anything bad. You can treat it as a signal to ask what in this theme is less visible right now or needs more attention.

Writing down your impressions in the journal can help. After a few weeks you may notice which themes come back and how your view changes. The value of this practice does not come from the cards being accurate, but from regularly pausing to think about your own life.

Remember that the cards cannot replace a conversation with the people close to you, or professional advice on matters of health, law or finance. Important decisions are best made on the basis of reliable information, and the cards can only be an inspiration for putting your thoughts in order.

Sources: Arthur Edward Waite, “The Pictorial Key to the Tarot”, 1910; Rachel Pollack, “Seventy-Eight Degrees of Wisdom”, 1980–1983; Helen Farley, “A Cultural History of Tarot”, I.B. Tauris, 2009.

title: On psychonumerology and the limits of this app
body:
The term psychonumerology appears in books, courses and guides, particularly in Poland, where this app originates, as the name of a strand that combines traditional number symbolism with the language of personal development and self-reflection. Despite the prefix psycho, it is not a branch of psychology or a clinical method. It has no recognised standards, no research confirming that it works, and no connection with the profession of psychologist or psychotherapist.

The number descriptions in the app draw on this general way of talking about numbers, but they have been written from scratch and are symbolic in character. They can be a prompt to ask yourself questions about your motivations, relationships or plans. They are not, however, a means of diagnosing personality, emotions or mental health, and they say nothing certain about your future.

That is why we encourage you to treat every description as a suggestion to be tested, not as the truth about yourself. If something does not fit, you can simply set it aside. If something moves you, it is worth asking why, and looking for the answer in your own experience, in conversation with the people close to you or in reliable sources.

The app does not replace professional help. If you have felt sad, anxious or overwhelmed for some time, or find it hard to cope with everyday life, it is worth talking to a doctor, psychologist or psychotherapist. Reaching out for support is a sensible step, not a sign of weakness.

If you are in emotional crisis, a free crisis line can help: for example 116 123 in Poland and in the United Kingdom and Ireland (Samaritans), or 988 in the United States. Opening hours and other ways of getting in touch can change, so check the operator's website for your country. If life or health is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number: 112 in the European Union, 999 in the United Kingdom, 911 in the United States.

Remember, too, that important decisions about health, money, work or relationships are best made on the basis of reliable information and a conversation with people you trust, not on the basis of a number or a card. Symbolism can accompany reflection, but it should not replace it.

Sources: Underwood Dudley, “Numerology: Or What Pythagoras Wrought”, Mathematical Association of America, 1997; Encyclopaedia Britannica, entry “numerology”; crisis line numbers as published by their operators (as of November 2026; please check that they are still current).

title: Repeating numbers (11:11, 222, 333…)
body:
Many people notice the same digits on a clock, a receipt or a number plate: 11:11, 222, 555. Popular numerology calls them “angel numbers” and treats them as a signal to pause for a moment. There is no evidence that they carry a message, but they can be a good prompt for reflection. Here are the traditional associations.

111: a new beginning. Pay attention to your thoughts and intentions; what you focus on grows.

222: balance and patience. Trust that things are falling into place, and look after your relationships.

333: creativity and support. Express yourself; you are not alone in this.

444: stability. You are building on good foundations, so stick to the plan.

555: change. Something is shifting; stay open to the new.

666: a return to balance. Check whether concern for material things is crowding out your loved ones and yourself.

777: reflection and intuition. A good time for learning and listening to yourself.

888: abundance and agency. Your efforts are beginning to bear fruit.

999: an ending. Something is coming to a close; let it go.

000: a full cycle and potential. A moment when everything is possible.

11:11: a moment of awareness. In the tradition it is a “gateway”: a moment to make a wish or to ask yourself what you really want.

12:12: the next step. An encouragement to get going with what you have planned.

If a number keeps coming back, instead of looking for a prediction in it, ask: what was I thinking about when I saw it?
